prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B051 first after reading the openings. The central idea is simple and beautiful: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift is the same for both clock states, and many atoms can be held tightly without disturbing the transition. That turned optical clocks into the most precise instruments ever built, and it was verified the way I trust, by independent laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) comparing clocks and agreeing at the 10^-18 level. The reach into fundamental questions is real and not only technological: tests of the constancy of constants, searches for dark matter, and relativistic geodesy where a height difference of a centimetre shows up as a clock shift. Four colleagues (Kroll, Pearce, Johansson and Olsson) place it in their top six, and all six members who ranked it name the same two people, which is rare. Katori and Ye is a compact, defensible pair, with Katori for the invention and first demonstration and Ye for taking the concept to record accuracy and stability and into the many-body regime.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to the committee's own history. Hall and Hansch (combs, 2005) and Wineland (ion clocks, 2012) already recognised the frequency-measurement and single-quantum-system clock lines, and a sceptic can say the lattice clock is an evolution of that lineage rather than a new door. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so recognition may look early. The priority history of the 2001-2003 lattice proposals (including Lemonde and others) is also something I cannot settle from memory, and Ye's credit is partly entangled with the frequency-comb and cold-molecule work for which he is also known. Ion-clock groups and the broader community (Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Derevianko and others) are not credited, so a two-person prize leaves out people who made decisive steps.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B051 eighth because the optical lattice clock overlaps with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize, and he is unsure of Ye's credit for the clock itself.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but I think it is a difference in kind. The 2012 prize was for controlling and measuring individual quantum systems, and a single ion gives a very stable but low-count-rate clock. The lattice clock solves a different problem: how to interrogate many neutral atoms simultaneously, free of Doppler and recoil shifts and with the perturbing trap cancelled, and this is what made 10^-18 stability reachable in hours instead of weeks. As for Ye, his group's Sr clock work (systematics control, and the Fermi-degenerate many-body clock where interactions have to be understood) is part of the clock achievement itself, separate from his role in combs. I agree the Ye attribution is the more delicate of the two, and I would want it written carefully in the citation.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B051 second and values it as an instrument and measurement achievement, but asks whether recognition should wait for the redefinition of the SI second and notes the overlap with 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I do not think we should tie the prize to a metrology-body decision. The physics result is established: multiple independent clocks agree at 10^-18. The redefinition roadmap is a consequence of the discovery, not a precondition for its worth, and waiting risks recognising it only when it has become routine. I accept the point about careful wording, so the citation should say 'invention and realization of optical lattice clocks' and not claim the redefinition. His top choice B009 I respect as a genuine new window, but I am less able to judge the credit problem of naming one person for a collaboration-scale discovery, and I find that harder than the two-name clock case.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B051 first as the clearest case where a new measurement capability changes what can be observed, with Katori and Ye as a compact pair, and asks whether ion clocks and lattice clocks are separate achievements.
responses.response: I largely agree with Stefan, with the qualification that we are both from the precision-measurement side and may be too fond of this type of result. On ion versus lattice clocks, I would treat them as separate achievements because the lattice clock rests on a distinct idea (the magic wavelength) rather than on the trapped-ion technique, but a reader of the citation will ask the question, so the citation should name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept explicitly. I would not extend the credit to Lemonde or the later JILA/NIST contributors without a strong archival reason, as that would push beyond a clean two-person prize.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B038 (circuit QED) first and discloses that he directs a national programme built on that architecture, flagging possible bias and recusal, and ranks B051 fifth.
responses.response: I respect that Goran stated his interest openly. On the science I agree circuit QED is a major conceptual transplant of cavity QED into a chip, and I ranked it eighth only because of timing and allocation, not because I doubt its importance. Four names for three places is a real difficulty (Blais, Girvin, Wallraff, Schoelkopf), and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon hard to defend to the wider community. I would not stop us from discussing it, but I think B038 is better kept as a later candidate than the preferred configuration this year. Given his programme, it would also be prudent for him to leave the allocation among the four credited names to the rest of us.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B027 first for ultracold-atom Hubbard simulation, with a clean model in direct contact with experiment, and acknowledges that choosing three of five credited names is a judgement.
responses.response: This is close to my own field and I am drawn to it, but I ranked it seventh because I am not sure the field has delivered one decisive discovery, in the sense of a result where nature surprised us. The Mott-insulator transition and the quantum gas microscope are impressive controls, but a good part of the impact is as a platform whose payoff in solving hard many-body problems is still partial, and the overlap with the Bose-Einstein condensation and laser-cooling prizes is large. The choice of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller over Cirac and Dalibard also seems arbitrary to me at this stage. I keep B027 as an alternative, not as the preferred choice, but I would listen if Bernhard can argue a specific decisive experiment.

uncertainties: Exact priority between Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength lattice proposal and parallel proposals (for example Lemonde and colleagues) needs a check against the original papers.
Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize.
How to word Ye's contribution so that it covers lattice-clock accuracy and many-body clock work and does not blur into the comb prize.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the SI second.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but that connection concerns attosecond physics and not the optical lattice clock work, and I have no personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye apparent from my profile. I work in atomic theory in a neighbouring area, so I might be sympathetic to atomic-physics candidates and I want colleagues to challenge me if so; I do not see this as requiring recusal on B051.
